beats.say: Open like a teacher: you started as one cell and now you are trillions; how? Playful. No questions.

lines.text: 1 cell  →  trillions of cells
lines.say: You began life as a single cell. Now you are made of trillions. And every day you replace old, worn-out cells. How do cells make more cells without making mistakes? Through mitosis.

beats.say: Mitosis: nuclear division giving two genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number. Four jobs: growth, repair, replacement, asexual reproduction. No questions.

lines.text: {{Mitosis|ul.p}}: division of the nucleus that makes cells with {{identical|ul}} genes and the {{same number of chromosomes|ul}}
lines.say: Mitosis is a way a cell divides its nucleus to make two new cells that are genetically identical to the original, with exactly the same number of chromosomes.

lines.text: growth      repair      replacing worn-out cells      asexual reproduction
lines.say: Cells use it for four jobs: growth, repair, replacing worn-out cells, and asexual reproduction.

beats.say: Use the picture: a cell with 4 chromosomes. They copy themselves into pairs of sister chromatids joined at a centromere, line up in the middle, are pulled apart to opposite ends, and two cells form each with 4 chromosomes. No questions.

lines.text: a body cell with 4 chromosomes
lines.say: Let's follow a cell that has four chromosomes. To keep things simple, the picture shows just four.

lines.text: step 1:  every chromosome COPIES itself
lines.say: Step one happens before the cell divides. Every chromosome makes an exact copy of its DNA.

lines.text: each chromosome is now 2 identical {{sister chromatids|ul.p}} joined at a {{centromere|ul}}
lines.say: Each chromosome is now two identical halves, called sister chromatids, joined in the middle at the centromere. It looks like an X.

lines.text: step 2:  the X shapes line up across the middle of the cell
lines.say: Step two: the X shapes line up across the middle of the cell, along its equator.

lines.text: step 3:  the sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite ends
lines.say: Step three: fibres pull the sister chromatids apart, one of each pair to each end of the cell.

lines.text: step 4:  two nuclei form, then the cell splits  →  2 daughter cells, each with 4 chromosomes
lines.say: Step four: a nucleus forms at each end, and the cell divides. We have two daughter cells, each with four chromosomes, identical to the parent.

beats.say: A friend says mitosis halves the chromosome number because one cell becomes two. Test with 46 human chromosomes: copied first, so each daughter gets 46. Detective tone, no questions.

lines.text: human body cell: 46 chromosomes
lines.say: A friend of mine says mitosis halves the chromosomes, because one cell becomes two. Let's test it with a human body cell, which has forty-six chromosomes.

lines.text: if 46 were just split in half, each cell would get only 23
lines.say: If the forty-six were simply shared out, each new cell would get only twenty-three. That would be a disaster, missing half its instructions.

lines.text: But the chromosomes copy FIRST: each daughter cell gets all 46
lines.say: But that's not what happens. The chromosomes copy themselves first, then the copies separate. So each daughter cell gets a full set of forty-six.

lines.text: Copy first  →  same number  (46 → 46)
lines.say: The key idea: copy first, then divide. The number stays the same.

beats.say: A friend says mitosis stops when you stop growing. Test with a cut skin: new cells must be made. Detective tone, no questions.

lines.text: adult:  finished growing, so mitosis stops?
lines.say: Another friend says mitosis stops once you're fully grown. Let's test it. Imagine you cut your finger.

lines.text: The gap must be filled with new skin cells
lines.say: The gap in your skin has to be filled with new cells, and the only way to make identical new cells is mitosis.

lines.text: Adults use mitosis every day: repair and replacing worn-out cells
lines.say: So adults use mitosis all the time, to heal wounds and to replace worn-out cells like skin and blood cells.

beats.say: A friend says mitosis makes sperm and egg cells. Test: gametes need half the chromosomes; mitosis keeps them the same. Detective tone, no questions.

lines.text: if mitosis made gametes:   egg 46  +  sperm 46
lines.say: A final friend says mitosis makes eggs and sperm. Let's test it with numbers. If both were made by mitosis, each would have forty-six chromosomes.

lines.text: at fertilisation:  46 + 46  =  92 in the baby
lines.say: Then at fertilisation the baby would start with ninety-two chromosomes. And the next generation would have even more. Impossible.

lines.text: Sex cells are made by a DIFFERENT division: meiosis, which halves the number
lines.say: So sex cells must be made by a different division, called meiosis, which halves the number. We'll meet it next. Mitosis is for growth and repair.

beats.say: Asexual reproduction: one parent, mitosis, identical offspring (clones). Example: a single-celled organism or a plant cutting. No questions.

lines.text: one parent  →  mitosis  →  identical offspring (clones)
lines.say: Mitosis is also how some organisms reproduce. With only one parent, the parent divides by mitosis, so the offspring are genetically identical to it. We call them clones.

lines.text: examples:  single-celled organisms,  plants grown from cuttings
lines.say: Single-celled organisms do this, and so do plants grown from cuttings.

beats.say: Do it TOGETHER: a cell with 6 chromosomes divides by mitosis twice. Questions written on the board first.

lines.text: a cell with 6 chromosomes divides by mitosis, then both daughter cells divide again
lines.say: Now you help me. A cell has six chromosomes and divides by mitosis. Then each of the two new cells divides again by mitosis.

lines.text: After the first division: 2 cells, each with 6 chromosomes
lines.say: Yes.

ask.prompt: After the first division, how many cells are there and how many chromosomes in each?
ask.onMiss: Ask: mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same. How many cells from one?

lines.text: After the second division: 4 cells, each with 6 chromosomes
lines.say: Yes.

ask.prompt: After the second division, how many cells are there and how many chromosomes in each?
ask.onMiss: Ask: each of the 2 cells makes 2 new cells. How many now?

beats.say: The child works alone: why mitosis is needed for healing; and what happens just before the cell divides. Hints only if stuck.

lines.text: a cut heals;   chromosomes must copy
lines.say: Your turn to lead.

lines.text: New identical cells are made by mitosis to fill the gap
lines.say: First.

ask.prompt: Why is mitosis needed to heal a cut?
ask.lookFor: It makes new, genetically identical cells to replace the lost ones.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what must fill the gap? What kind of cells?

lines.text: Each chromosome copies itself into two sister chromatids
lines.say: Second.

ask.prompt: What happens to each chromosome before the cell divides?
ask.lookFor: It copies itself, making two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
ask.onMiss: Ask: if the cell divided without copying, what would each new cell be missing?

board.text: Say it in your own words

lines.text: copy first,  then divide
lines.say: Last one.

ask.prompt: Why must the chromosomes copy before the cell divides, if the daughter cells are to keep the full set?
ask.lookFor: Without copying, the chromosomes would be shared out and each daughter cell would get only half; copying first gives each a complete identical set.
ask.onMiss: Ask: if you tear a book in two, do both halves have the whole story?
